payload.body_text:
An agent should not keep its authority when the doctrine that earned it has expired.

Doctrine is strategy made executable: the current diagnosis, tradeoffs, anti-goals, kill criteria, and escalation conditions. It has a half-life because those premises change.

Suppose a support agent can issue account credits without review under doctrine version 12. Pricing policy changes in version 13, but the permission survives. The agent can now execute obsolete judgment perfectly—and at customer speed. That is coherent wrongness, not model failure.

Permissions should be bound to a doctrine version, an owner, and a freshness window. When that doctrine ages or is superseded, authority should fall back from autonomous action to draft, approval, or stop.

When the map expires, permission to act from it should expire too.

novel_idea.topic_thesis: Autonomous permissions should expire with the doctrine version that justified them.
novel_idea.angle: Treat doctrine freshness as a condition of authority, not as documentation hygiene: when the map ages, the agent’s permission to act from it should decay too.
novel_idea.hook: The most dangerous agent may be the one that keeps obeying after its doctrine has expired.
novel_idea.argument_summary: Agent permissions are usually granted based on capability and reviewed only after failure. But autonomous action is authorized by a particular set of premises, tradeoffs, and boundaries. As that doctrine ages, faithful execution can become coherent wrongness: the agent remains aligned while the organization’s map stops matching reality. Operators should therefore bind permissions to a named doctrine version and its expected half-life, then require revalidation or automatically reduce authority when that doctrine becomes stale. This differs from the prior Context Checksum argument, which gates permission increases on initial strategic agreement. The new claim governs authority after deployment: permission must decay over time even when outputs remain accurate and no visible disagreement has appeared.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest post argues that humans and machines must pass the same Context Checksum before permissions expand. This argument introduces a different mechanism and operator decision: doctrine has a half-life, so previously justified permissions can become unsafe without any checksum divergence or capability failure. It replaces one-time authorization with version-bound, expiring authority.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The source defines Doctrine Half-Life as how long doctrine remains valid and understood; warns that stale doctrine can regulate confidently from a false model; identifies coherent wrongness as faithful action from false premises; asks who is accountable when doctrine ages but an agent keeps acting; and states that permissions should rise only as doctrine, evaluations, and boundary feedback mature.

novel_idea.topic_thesis: Autonomous permissions should not outlive the doctrine version that justified them.
novel_idea.angle: Shift agent governance from one-time authorization to continuing validity: autonomy must contract when doctrine becomes stale, disputed, or superseded.
novel_idea.hook: The most dangerous agent may be executing yesterday’s strategy with permissions granted yesterday—and no expiration date.
novel_idea.argument_summary: Organizations usually treat permission as durable once an agent proves capable. But capability can remain high while doctrine ages. An agent may then execute obsolete premises faithfully, creating customer promises, code changes, or financial commitments after the organization’s map has changed. The operator decision is to bind consequential permissions to a current, owned, versioned doctrine source and withdraw or reduce them when that doctrine becomes stale or is replaced. This differs from checking alignment before expanding access: it addresses the decay of authorization after deployment, when nothing technically fails but the strategic basis for autonomy has expired.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest post argues that humans and machines should pass a Context Checksum before an agent receives broader permissions. This new argument concerns what happens afterward: permissions that were once coherent become dangerous when doctrine ages. The substantive delta is permission revocation based on doctrine freshness, not pre-deployment alignment testing. It introduces a different causal mechanism and operator decision: autonomy must contract as its governing premises lose validity.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The source defines doctrine half-life as how long doctrine remains valid, current, and understood before drift or world change makes it stale. It states that agents require current doctrine, canonical retrieval, permissions, stop conditions, and update ownership; asks who is accountable if doctrine ages while an agent keeps acting; and warns that stale doctrine can turn a regulator into a disturbance generator. The Minimum Viable Coherence Program also requires doctrine versions, owners, permission levels, doctrine-to-agent interfaces, and updates to every affected agent and workflow when doctrine changes.

payload.angle: Shift agent governance from one-time authorization to continuing validity: autonomy must contract when doctrine becomes stale, disputed, or superseded.
payload.hook: An agent can be perfectly obedient and still become dangerous overnight.
payload.body_text:
An agent can be perfectly obedient and still become dangerous overnight.

Doctrine has a half-life: the period during which its diagnosis, tradeoffs, and instructions remain valid. Yet most permissions survive long after that doctrine becomes stale, disputed, or superseded.

A pricing agent authorized under version 12 may keep issuing discounts after version 13 changes the margin strategy. It did not hallucinate. It followed obsolete premises with valid credentials.

Permissions should therefore bind to a specific doctrine version and its continuing validity. When that doctrine ages or enters dispute, autonomy should contract: external action becomes draft-only, irreversible action stops, escalation returns to a human.

Authorization cannot be a one-time event. If the doctrine expires, the permission must expire with it.
